title: Koh Samui Attractions 2026 — Beaches, Big Buddha, Ang Thong | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: The best things to do on Koh Samui, Thailand — Chaweng and Lamai beaches, Big Buddha, Hin Ta Hin Yai rocks, Fisherman's Village, and Ang Thong Marine Park, with real entry fees, opening hours, and what to know before you go.
keywords: Koh Samui attractions, Chaweng Beach, Lamai Beach, Big Buddha Samui, Hin Ta Hin Yai, Ang Thong, Bophut
intro: Koh Samui is bigger than most people expect. Loop around the island and you'll find white-sand beaches, hilltop temples, oddly shaped rocks, an old fishing village, and a marine park you have to take a boat out to reach. We've pulled together the spots that were actually worth the trip, with real entry fees and the things you'll want to know, so you can plan your whole island loop in one place.

blocks.html: Samui packs a lot of different trips into one island. Beach people get long stretches of sand along the east coast; if you're into temples or photo spots, there are shrines and viewpoints; and anyone who wants to get out on the water can take a boat to Ang Thong. This guide runs zone by zone — starting with the popular beaches, moving through the temples and natural spots, and finishing with the boat trip out to the islands, plus a short sample plan you can adapt yourself.

blocks.text: Chaweng and Lamai — the two main east-coast beaches

blocks.html: Chaweng is the longest and liveliest beach on the island — fine white sand, clear water, and a continuous run of restaurants, bars, and places to stay along the back of it. It suits anyone who wants the beach plus some nightlife. Lamai sits just to the south, quieter and more laid-back, better if you'd rather sunbathe somewhere calm.

items: Chaweng — the longest, busiest beach, packed with restaurants and live music at night, with a wide range of stays from guesthouses to beachfront resorts
Lamai — quieter, soft sand, good for sunbathing and swimming, with the Hin Ta Hin Yai rocks at the southern end
Both beaches are free — no entry fee, though some beachfront bars set a minimum spend if you want to use their loungers

blocks.title: Before you get in the water
blocks.html: During Samui's monsoon season (roughly Oct–Dec) the sea can get rough and cloudy, and some days there are warning flags up. Always check the forecast and look for the beach flags before going in. The east coast — Chaweng and Lamai — tends to catch more of the swell during this period than the other sides of the island.

blocks.text: Big Buddha (Wat Phra Yai), the north-coast landmark

blocks.html: The Big Buddha temple sits on a small island off the north coast near Bophut, with a large golden seated Buddha around 12 metres tall that you can spot from a distance when your plane comes in to land or as you arrive by boat. Climb the naga staircase to pay your respects at the top and you'll get sea views all around as well.

items: Opening hours — roughly 06:00–18:00 daily, free entry (there's a donation box if you'd like to give)
Dress code — cover your shoulders and knees, and take your shoes off before going up into the building, the same as any Thai temple
Nearby — pair it with Wat Plai Laem, which is a short drive away, in the same trip

blocks.title: When to go
blocks.html: Go in the morning or toward late afternoon — the sun is gentler and it's less crowded than midday. Bring a shoulder wrap in case you've turned up in a sleeveless top, so you don't have to borrow one on the spot.

blocks.text: Hin Ta Hin Yai, the oddly shaped rocks at the end of Lamai

blocks.html: Hin Ta Hin Yai is a cluster of seaside granite rocks at the southern end of Lamai beach, weathered by nature into shapes that resemble male and female genitals — which is exactly why so many people stop to take photos. There's a local legend tying them to a grandfather and grandmother whose boat wrecked on the way to ask for a girl's hand in marriage. It's also one of the island's prettier sunset spots.

items: Free entry — walk down from the car park past the souvenir stalls straight to the rocks
Watch your footing — the rocks get wet and mossy, so shoes with grippy soles help, and don't climb out where the waves reach
Combine it — it's right by Lamai beach, so you can roll it into the same part of your day

blocks.html: Bophut is an old neighbourhood on the island's north coast, and its highlight is the Fisherman's Village — a narrow seaside street lined with old wooden buildings, restaurants, cafés, bars, and shops. It's a pleasant stroll any day of the week, and it gets especially busy on Friday nights when it turns into a walking street.

items: Friday walking street — opens Friday evenings, roughly 17:00–23:00, with food, souvenirs, clothes, and live music (the road closes to traffic on Fridays — it's walking only)
Weekdays — the shops are still open and it's an easy stroll, with fewer people than Friday
Dinner by the sea — there are seafood restaurants and sea-view cafés where you can settle in for the sunset

blocks.text: Nature spots — Na Muang Waterfall and Lad Koh viewpoint

blocks.html: If you want a break from the beach and some nature in the island's interior, Na Muang Waterfall sits in the middle of Samui. It has two tiers — the first is an easy drive up to, the second takes a bit of a walk into the forest — and entry is free. Lad Koh viewpoint is on the coastal road between Chaweng and Lamai, an easy place to pull over and photograph the bay.

items: Na Muang Waterfall — open roughly 09:00–18:00, free entry · tier 2 means a forest walk, and the path is slippery in the rain, so wear trainers
Lad Koh viewpoint — free entry, with a pavilion and a path down to the clifftop, looking over the east-coast bay
A note on elephants — around Na Muang you'll be offered elephant trekking, and some operators raise concerns about animal welfare, so skip it if it doesn't sit right with you

blocks.text: Ang Thong Marine Park — the boat trip out to the islands

blocks.html: If you have a full day to spare, Ang Thong National Marine Park is Samui's big day out on the water. It's an archipelago of more than 40 limestone islands, with an emerald sea inside the mountains (a saltwater lake in the middle of the main island), clifftop viewpoints, white-sand beaches, and snorkelling spots. It's a roughly 1–2 hour boat ride out from Samui, depending on the type of boat.

items: Park entry fee — around 300 THB for adults, 150 THB for children (most tours include this already, but check before you book)
Big boat — from around 1,000–1,400 THB/person, comfortable to ride and takes longer to get there, better if you get seasick easily
Speedboat — from around 1,800–2,500 THB/person, faster and gives you more time on the islands, but a bumpier ride
Activities — hiking up to viewpoints, kayaking, and snorkelling, depending on the package

blocks.title: Before you book a boat trip
blocks.html: Ang Thong closes for part of the monsoon season (usually around Nov–Dec), and trips can be cancelled if the sea gets rough · tour prices swing with the season and group size. Always check the forecast, the operator's reputation, and the life jackets before you get on the boat. If you get seasick easily, take something about half an hour before you set off.

faq.q: How many days do you need to make a Koh Samui trip worthwhile?
faq.a: If you want to hit the beaches, the temples, the nature spots, and the Ang Thong boat trip, plan on at least 3 days and 2 nights. Spend the first day on the north zone and the beaches, the second inland and on the south side, and keep the third for a full day out at Ang Thong. If you only have 1–2 days, stick to the beaches and Big Buddha first.

faq.q: Which Koh Samui attractions are free to visit?
faq.a: A lot of them are free — Chaweng beach, Lamai beach, Big Buddha, Hin Ta Hin Yai, the Fisherman's Village in Bophut, Na Muang Waterfall, and Lad Koh viewpoint. The main thing that costs money is Ang Thong National Marine Park (around 300 THB park entry for adults, plus the boat tour fee).

faq.q: How much does Ang Thong cost from Samui, and how do you book it?
faq.a: Big-boat trips start at around 1,000–1,400 THB/person, and speedboats start at around 1,800–2,500 THB/person. Prices swing with the season and group size. Most include the park entry fee, but check before you book. Choose a reputable operator and be prepared for the trip to be moved or cancelled if the sea is rough during the monsoon.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to visit Samui?
faq.a: The clearest skies and calmest seas usually run from around February to April. Samui's heavy monsoon tends to arrive from around October to December, with rough seas and a lot of rain, when boat trips can be cancelled fairly often. If you come during this stretch, keep your plans flexible and check the forecast day by day.

faq.q: What's the best way to get around Koh Samui?
faq.a: The island is fairly big and the sights are spread out, so a lot of people rent a motorbike for the freedom. But some stretches of road are steep and winding — ride carefully and wear a helmet. If motorbikes aren't your thing, a rental car, taxis, or songthaews (shared pickups) all work. Some sights are far apart, so it's worth mapping your route out by zone.
